posts.title: Why we clean every record twice
posts.excerpt: Every record that enters Enban Records goes through a dry brush and an ultrasonic bath before it reaches the counter or the crate.
posts.content:
When Ines Valdane founded Enban Records in 2014 at 7 Weir Lane in Easterby, she established a single core rule for the shop: we only sell records that have been played on our own counter. Over the past decade, that rule has shaped how we buy, how we grade, and how we care for the 6,000 discs in our bins. But playing every record on our listening desk turntable introduces an inescapable reality. Every piece of pre-owned vinyl carries the physical history of its previous homes, including airborne dust, skin oils, paper particles from deteriorating inner sleeves, and dried residues from old cleaning solutions. If you put an unwashed record onto a turntable, the diamond stylus acts like a microscopic plow, compacting dirt into the delicate groove walls and eroding high-frequency information.

To protect both our listening desk equipment and our customers' home setups, our technician Rafael Ortega cleans every used record twice before it is priced and sleeved. This routine takes place at our workshop bench behind the counter, long before a disc is placed into the bins or added to today's 17:00 arrival crate. The two-stage method is not an aesthetic ritual or an exercise in perfectionism. It is a mechanical necessity based on how microscopic debris interacts with vinyl grooves under high stylus pressure.

The first stage is a dry carbon-fibre pass. Before any liquid or bath is introduced, Rafael uses an anti-static carbon-fibre brush across the rotating disc to lift loose, dry surface contaminants. If you apply liquid to a dusty record immediately, surface dust turns into an abrasive slurry that settles deeper into the groove valleys. The fine carbon fibres discharge residual static electricity on the polyvinyl surface while gently sweeping away hair, loose paper dust, and pet dander. Once the surface is clear of loose particles, the record is ready for its deep liquid treatment.

The second stage is an ultrasonic bath. Standard record cleaning machines rely on vacuum suction and velvet lips, which can occasionally press grit against the delicate groove walls or leave micro-scratches on soft vinyl compounds. In our workshop, Rafael lowers the record into a tank filled with purified, distilled water mixed with a tiny measure of non-ionic wetting agent. The ultrasonic transducers emit high-frequency sound waves through the liquid, generating millions of microscopic cavitation bubbles. When these bubbles collapse against the vinyl, they produce focused shockwaves that dislodge deep-seated mold, dried nicotine, finger grease, and stubborn pressing residues from the bottom of the groove.

Because the cavitation occurs in liquid without mechanical friction, the ultrasonic bath cleans without wearing down the delicate groove modulations. After several minutes in the tank, the disc is lifted, carefully dried with filtered air, and inspected under bright tungsten bench lighting. Only albums that pass this inspection and grade at Very Good Plus (VG+) or higher make their way into our shop.

Finally, the original paper inner sleeve—which often harbors decades of abrasive dust—is replaced with a fresh, anti-static poly-lined inner liner. When Mira Lindqvist pulls up to twelve albums for your afternoon listening appointment, or when you pick up a newly arrived reissue from the 17:00 crate, you can place the tonearm down knowing that the groove is clean, silent, and true to the music pressed into it.

posts.title: Building a first shelf of twelve
posts.excerpt: How Mira chooses twelve records for someone who has never owned a turntable.
posts.content:
When someone books the desk with no record collection at all, Mira starts from what they already listen to, not from what a shop thinks everyone should own. Twelve records is enough to hear four or five kinds of music without feeling hurried.

The €6 is credited to anything you buy, and the ones you do not choose go straight back into the bins. Most people leave with one or two, and a better idea of what to ask for next time.
